newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan stocks to consolidate, watch yen.
newsitem.headline: Japan stocks to consolidate, watch yen.

text.p: Japanese stocks are likely to consolidate recent gains in the coming week and may even push further beyond the 20,000 point level, brokers said.
But they warned that currency turbulence, which knocked the wind out of export issues in the past week, needed to be watched carefully.
"There is a fair amount of volatility in the currency market which means that time will be needed for calm to return," said Masaaki Higashida, strategist at Nomura Securities.

"Volatility in currencies has the potential to dampen the optimism of firms in their business outlook and earnings and, in turn, it could even chill capital investment plans which hold the key to the health of the economy."

The Nikkei average started the previous week at a new high for the year of 20,489.75 but was buffeted by the yen, which surged past 112 yen to the dollar during the week, as well as by official discount rate increase jitters.

On Friday, the 225-share average rose 131.61 points or 0.66 percent, clawing above the 20,000 line to end at 20,009.00 as buying of exporter issues revived on relief that currencies seemed to have settled down.
"On a valuation basis, high-techs are really the only issues investors can buy with confidence in the long term," said Shinichi Ishikawa, Credit Lyonnais Securities strategist.
"Once currencies settle down, buying in the sector should pick up and provide the indices with support," he added.

Some brokers said pension fund money which boosted indices in recent weeks was beginning to ebb and fundamentals were not as robust as before. But they added that foreign investors were still net buyers and pension funds still had the potential to buy.

"Pension fund buying is not as active and profit-taking moves are appearing," said Katsuhiko Kodama, Toyo Securities general manager. "But funds are not bound for bonds, so pensions should resume their stock purchases once they have secured profits."
Brokers said apart from currencies, attention would be on corporate earnings, which are in full swing, as well as industrial production data, which will be released on May 29.

"The market is beginning to realise that the stifling effect of the two percentage point rise in consumption tax, which went into effect April 1, is not as terrible as envisioned," said a broker at a "Big Four" brokerage.
"But it remains to be seen when the tax increase effect will wear off and investors are hoping for clues from the economic data," he added.
Brokers said that the near-term goal for the Nikkei would be to close above the recent closing high of near 20,500.
